rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-IV, Tables I-VII, Figs 5-11 - the authors built three data-logger devices with low-cost resistive sensors, ran two calibration experiments in clay soil with gravimetric reference and a 19 April-3 May 2016 pot evaluation comparing sensor readings against weight-based moisture, reporting percent errors.
rows.notes: The study reports only sensor accuracy/precision (calibration curves, percent error averaging 13.7-30% across three devices, sources of error: corrosion, ion concentration, temperature, installation). It does not run any irrigation scheduling, measure water applied or saved, or assess water-use efficiency, and does not study farmers in developing regions; the 10% application-efficiency gain mentioned in the Introduction is cited from another work [5], not the authors' own result. The study's own conclusion is that these sensors are not recommended for continuous monitoring or high-accuracy irrigation control, which if anything cuts against the claimed benefit. Sensor accuracy is a precondition of the claimed water-efficiency effect, so this is upstream evidence. Low cost is asserted as a premise, not measured.

notes: Full conference paper text available; short pot/greenhouse experiment on one clay soil with three sensor units and no crop or irrigation outcome measured.
